p: Kulasegaram Vairamuthu Pandara Vanniyan was a native of the Vanni and is said to have reigned there from 1785. Much about his family is unclear, but reports give him a sister, Nallanachal Vanniyan, and two younger brothers who served as his minister and his commander. He married into the family of Kumarasinghe Maha Vanniya of Nuwara Wewa, and so gained political power in the southern Vanni as well as the north. He is said to have lived at Kumulamunai, in the present Mullaitivu District.

The Vanni served as a buffer zone between the north and south of Sri Lanka. After the Portuguese captured the Jaffna Kingdom in 1621 the region was under their nominal control, and around 1782 the Dutch defeated the Vanniar chieftains.

Pandara Vanniyan is said to have defeated the Dutch officer Lieutenant von Driberg several times. Against the British, the Vanniars carried on a predatory warfare in Mannar and Trincomalee and reached the Jaffna Peninsula, and the British built forts to keep them at bay. In alliance with the Kandy Kingdom he rose to expel the British from his district. On 25 August 1803 he attacked the Government House at Mullaitivu, drove out the garrison under Captain Edward Mudge of the 19th Regiment and seized the fort and its cannons. He then overran the northern districts as far as Elephant Pass.

He turned from conventional warfare to guerrilla tactics, but the British organised a three-pronged attack from Jaffna, Mannar and Trincomalee. Von Driberg, who had stayed on after the British ousted the Dutch, defeated him on 31 October 1803 at Katsilaimadu, capturing a cannon given to him by the Kandyan king Sri Wickrema Rajasinghe. His houses were burned and his people dispersed into the jungle and out of the Vanni.

No longer a ruler, Pandara Vanniyan withdrew to areas near the Kandy Kingdom. Accounts of his end differ: by one he died fighting the British, by another he remained there until September 1810, when British forces ambushed him, and later died of his injuries. Von Driberg set up a granite monument at Katsilaimadu recording the defeat; in 2010 it was found broken. Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa declared him a national hero in 1982, and a statue stands in Vavuniya. Tamil nationalists honour him as an epic hero, and he is the subject of a novel by M. Karunanidhi and of a play by Mullaimani Ve Cuppiramaniyam that won a prize from the Ceylon Art Council in 1964.

notes: Death date conflict: the article's lead says he reigned 1785-1803 and 'died battling the British', but its Death section says he survived the defeat of October 1803 and died after an ambush in September 1810. The existing entry has 'd. 1803'. I followed the Death section.
The article is poorly sourced and partly legendary in tone ('it is said', 'alternative histories'); I hedged accordingly. It calls von Driberg both a Dutch lieutenant and (on the monument) a captain.
The monument's inscription gives 31 October 1803; the article's text gives the place as Oddusuddan, Katsilaimadu.
The article spells the place Mullaitheevu; I used Mullaitivu as in the existing description and the article's own 'Mullaitivu District'.
